Artificial turf cleaning service in Kissimmee, Florida An artificial turf cleaning service rinses, power brooms and deodorizes turf so it drains, smells and looks the way it did on installation day. In Kissimmee, a basic visit runs roughly $80 to $150 and a deep clean with pet-odor treatment runs $150 to $400, based on published 2026 market ranges. Central Florida's oak leaf drop, pollen and lovebug seasons all shape the schedule. Reviewed by Luis Austin , owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026 What maintenance does artificial turf need? Artificial turf needs a hose rinse every week or two, power brooming a few times a year to lift matted pile, and a deeper sanitizing clean twice a year timed around Central Florida's live oak leaf drop and rainy season. Storms and heavy pollen weeks call for an extra pass in between. None of it involves an in-ground sprinkler; the state synthetic turf rule doesn't allow one to water turf at all. Artificial turf maintenance calendar for Central Florida Frequency Task Why it matters here Weekly (pet yards), every other week otherwise Hose rinse and a quick debris check Central Florida heat turns urine into odor fast; Rule 62-308.100 bars using an in-ground irrigation system on turf, so every rinse here is by hose Monthly Power broom against the grain, check infill depth Regular traffic and lovebug season, roughly April–May and again August–September in Florida, mat the pile down and leave residue that needs brushing out Twice a year, spring and fall Deep clean: sanitizing rinse, infill top-up, edge and seam check Timed around the live oak leaf drop in late winter into early spring and just ahead of the June–September rainy season After named storms or heavy pollen weeks Rake off debris, rinse the pollen film, check for standing water Afternoon storms can drop one to three inches an hour; spring pollen coats turf in a yellow film a plain rinse lifts Live oak timing from UF/IFAS live oak information ; lovebug seasons from UF/IFAS Extension on lovebugs . How often should pet turf be cleaned? Dog turf needs a hose rinse most days at the spot a dog actually uses, and at least once a week across the whole run, because Central Florida heat turns bacteria in urine into odor within hours. Beyond that, plan on a professional deep clean with an enzyme or antimicrobial treatment every three to four months, sooner with more than one dog or a yard that stays shaded and damp. Pet turf systems built with a fully permeable backing and zeolite or an antimicrobial-coated sand hold up longer between professional visits than regular lawn turf pressed into service as a dog run. This guide covers what to try if odor has already set in. Who needs a professional visit, and who just needs a hose An artificial turf cleaning service covers pet odor removal, turf deodorizing, power brooming, an infill top-up, turf sanitizing, and an enzyme cleaner worked into the backing where plain water doesn't reach. A homeowner's own rinse-and-broom routine covers most yards for the first year or two: hose it down, brush the high-traffic path, blow off leaves before they break down into the infill. A professional visit earns its cost once infill has visibly thinned, pet odor survives a normal rinse, or the pile in a traffic lane has matted down and stopped standing back up on its own. Vacation rentals are the other common case: a cleaning pass between a heavy booking stretch keeps the yard looking like the listing photos without the owner managing it long-distance. It's not worth booking a professional clean for turf under a year old with no pets and no visible problem; that money is better spent on nothing at all until there's something to actually fix. What a cleaning visit actually does Here's the sequence on a standard visit, start to finish. Walk the yard first. Check for matting, staining, low spots holding water, and any seam or edge that needs a separate repair call before cleaning goes ahead of it. Clear debris before water touches it. Leaves, acorns and lovebug residue get raked or blown off dry; wetting them first just presses them into the infill. Power broom against the grain. Lifts flattened pile and works old, compacted infill loose so it can be topped up evenly instead of layered over. Treat odor at the source. An enzyme or antimicrobial solution goes down into the infill and backing, not just across the top of the blades. Top up infill to depth. Brought back to roughly the original one to two pounds per square foot rather than left thin where it's washed or blown away. Final hose rinse and brush. A steady hose, not a high-pressure wand aimed to blast a section clean, which can strip infill and fray blade tips. What turf cleaning costs Published 2026 market ranges put a basic maintenance visit, rinse, debris removal and a power brooming, at $80 to $150 ( a national cleaning-cost survey ). A standard deep clean with infill work runs $150 to $400, and most homes land between $200 and $350. Pet-odor and sanitizing treatments sit toward the top of that range, because the enzyme product and the labor to work it into the infill cost more than a plain rinse. Heat, pollen and lovebugs: cleaning turf through a Central Florida year Heat is why pet odor here needs more attention than the same yard would in a cooler climate; warmth speeds up the bacteria that turn urine into smell, so a rinse schedule that works up north isn't enough in Kissimmee. Live oaks drop their old leaves as new growth comes in, typically late winter into early spring ( UF/IFAS live oak information ), and the tannins in a pile of wet oak leaves can stain turf fiber if they sit through a few afternoon storms. Florida runs two lovebug swarms a year, spring and again in late summer ( UF/IFAS Extension on lovebugs ), and their residue is acidic enough to dull turf color if it bakes in the sun instead of getting rinsed off within a day or two. Rainy season, June through September, does some of the cleaning for free by washing dust and pollen off the blades, but it also carries loose debris into low spots where Kissimmee's sandy base has settled, so those spots need an extra pass after a heavy storm. Does cleaning affect drainage rules? Florida's synthetic turf standard requires an installed lawn to stay permeable and not increase runoff onto a neighbor's property ( a summary of the state standard ). Infill packed solid with years of dust, pollen and pet waste can slow how fast water actually gets through the backing, even though the product itself is still rated for the same drainage. Regular power brooming and an infill top-up are what keep the real-world drainage close to the rated manufacturer specification of more than 30 inches an hour , which matters most on lots near a pond or swale, where the state standard already limits how close turf can sit to the water. What a rushed cleaning job misses A pressure washer aimed at the turf instead of a hose is the most common shortcut, and it can blow infill out of a section, fray blade tips, and on an older lawn loosen a seam that a gentler rinse would have left alone. Skipping the debris pass and going straight to water just presses leaves and lovebug residue deeper into the pile instead of removing them. Spraying a deodorizer on top of the blades without working it into the infill treats the smell for a few days and misses where the odor actually comes from. And a clean that skips the infill top-up leaves the backing exposed in traffic lanes, which shows up as a dull, thin-looking stripe within a season. Between visits Rinse pet areas with a hose a few times a week between professional visits, more often at the peak of a Florida summer. Brush high-traffic paths against the grain every month or two so the pile keeps standing up on its own. Rake or blow off leaves and lovebug residue within a day or two rather than letting an afternoon storm work them into the infill. This guide covers debris season in more detail. If a spot keeps re-staining or smelling no matter how often it's rinsed, that's usually a sign for a repair visit rather than another cleaning. How do you find the best turf cleaning company near me? Ask what's actually included: a rinse and a broom is not the same service as an enzyme treatment worked into the infill, and the price should say which one you're getting. Ask whether infill gets topped up as part of the visit or billed separately, since a clean that leaves infill thin looks worse within weeks. And ask how they handle water pressure; a company that can't explain why it uses a hose instead of a pressure washer probably hasn't thought about what a blast of water does to years-old backing. Tell us the yard size, whether pets use it, and when it was last cleaned, and we'll quote the visit. Osceola County Kissimmee Buenaventura Lakes Celebration St. Cloud Poinciana Reunion ChampionsGate Four Corners Harmony Orange County Hunters Creek Meadow Woods Southchase Lake Nona Dr. Phillips Polk County Davenport Questions people ask How long after a cleaning visit can pets or kids use the yard again? Usually right away for a basic rinse and broom. If an enzyme or sanitizing treatment was applied, give it fifteen to twenty minutes to sit before heavy use, and a bit longer in shade where things dry more slowly. Does turf cleaning remove old pet odor completely? Often, if the odor is in the infill and hasn't reached the backing or the base underneath. Odor that survives a proper deep clean and a fresh infill swap usually means urine has worked past the infill, which points toward replacement rather than another cleaning. Can I clean artificial turf myself between professional visits? Yes, and it's the better routine. A hose rinse, a stiff push broom used against the grain, and prompt removal of leaves and debris cover most of what turf needs between the twice-yearly deep cleans. What's the difference between power brooming and brushing? Power brooming uses a machine, usually a walk-behind unit with rotating bristles, to lift matted pile and loosen packed infill across a large area quickly. Hand brushing with a stiff broom does the same job on a smaller scale or in tight corners a machine can't reach. Do you top up infill during a regular cleaning visit? Yes, when it's visibly thin. Infill migrates and compacts over time from rinsing, rain and foot traffic, and a clean that only rinses and broomes without restoring the depth leaves the backing more exposed than before. How soon after a storm should turf be cleaned? Within a few days if debris or standing water is visible. Leaves and organic matter left wet against the blades start to break down and stain the fiber faster in Florida heat than they would in a cooler climate. Will cleaning turf void a warranty from the original installer? A hose rinse and gentle power brooming shouldn't affect a manufacturer's warranty; those cover UV fade and material defects, not maintenance. A pressure washer or harsh chemical could, so ask the original installer what the warranty language actually excludes before using either. ## Artificial Turf Replacement in Kissimmee, FL
URL: https://kissimmeeartificialturf.com/turf-replacement/
Updated: 2026-09-21

Artificial turf replacement in Kissimmee, Florida Artificial turf replacement means pulling out a worn-out lawn, correcting the base underneath it, and laying a new surface, usually once a lawn is ten to fifteen years into Florida's sun. A full tear-out and rebuild prices close to a new install; a sound base that only needs the old turf removed trims a meaningful share off that. Most jobs also bring an older install up to the current state turf standard. Reviewed by Luis Austin , owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026 Repair or replace? What the base tells you Artificial turf replacement means old turf removal, a base rebuild where it's needed, honest turf disposal, and a re-turf that upgrades the product you had rather than a like-for-like swap. The condition of what's underneath, not just how the lawn looks, is what should decide between a repair and a full replacement. Repair or replace: reading the signs What you see Repair candidate Replace candidate Why A single open seam or a small burn patch Yes Not necessary Isolated failure; the rest of the base and turf are still sound Widespread fading and brittle blades across the whole lawn No, a patch won't match Yes The fiber itself has UV-degraded; that doesn't repair, it only gets replaced Multiple soft, sunken or spongy spots at 12+ years old Rarely worth it Usually The base has likely failed in more than one place, not only where it shows Pet odor that survives a deep clean and fresh infill No Yes Often means the backing or an old fabric weed barrier underneath is holding urine Turf installed before the 2026 state standard, irrigation still capped underneath N/A Worth doing at the same time Replacement is the practical moment to remove old heads and anchor edges to the current rule What survives a replacement, and what doesn't A base that's still flat, well-drained and at the right depth doesn't need to be dug out and redone; that's the single biggest cost difference between a replacement and a first-time install. We probe it in a few spots, check for soft or wet areas, and reuse what's still doing its job while adding and recompacting where it's thinned. Edging often survives too. A bender-board or paver border holds up longer than the turf inside it, so a still-solid edge gets reused rather than pulled for no reason. What doesn't survive: the turf itself, obviously, along with any fabric weed barrier from an older pet install, since that's usually the thing holding years of urine odor. Old irrigation heads that were simply capped rather than removed get addressed properly this time, since the current standard doesn't allow an in-ground system to water turf at all. Infill is the other thing worth checking before assuming it can stay: the current state standard only allows crumb rubber or another synthetic infill inside the footprint of playground equipment, so an older lawn or general play area filled with rubber or TPE gets refilled with clean silica sand, zeolite or a coated sand during the replacement. Ten to fifteen years of Florida sun, up close Turf in Florida generally lasts ten to twenty years depending on UV stabilization, traffic and infill ( industry lifespan data ), and the low end of that range is common on unshaded Central Florida lawns that see full sun most of the year. What worn-out looks like by then: blades gone from green to a washed-out gray-green, brittle rather than springy underfoot; infill migrated or compacted so the backing shows through in traffic lanes; a surface that's stopped bouncing back after someone walks across it. A lawn that hit those marks five years ago and is only now getting replaced usually has base problems layered on top of the fiber problems, part of why the quote is rarely just the cost of new material. This guide breaks lifespan down by use and product. How a replacement job runs The sequence differs from a first-time install mainly in the first step. We evaluate what's underneath first. Pull back a corner, probe the base for depth and moisture, and decide how much of it is worth keeping before pricing anything. Old turf comes out. Cut into sections, rolled, and hauled off; a large yard can mean several thousand pounds of material leaving the site. The base gets corrected, not just reused blindly. Low spots are regraded, thinned base gets built back up, and the whole area is recompacted in lifts even where most of it stayed. New turf goes in to the current standard. A product with no intentionally added PFAS or heavy metals, edges and seams anchored the way Rule 62-308.100 requires. Irrigation is capped properly. Any head that survived the old install, even one that was already turned off, gets capped at the line rather than left in place. Final grade and drainage check. We confirm the 1 to 2 percent slope away from the house still holds before the last section of turf goes down. What artificial turf replacement costs Artificial turf replacement is quoted per job rather than off a fixed rate, but it prices closer to a first-time install than to a repair, because most of the labor, demo, base work, new turf, repeats either way. A full tear-out and rebuild often lands near the lower-to-middle part of the usual Central Florida installed range, roughly $8–$18 a square foot, and a base that only needs light correction can trim a meaningful share off that. What raises it: hauling a large volume of old turf and infill off site, a base that failed in more than one area, and capping or rerouting irrigation left in place under the old lawn. What lowers it: a base that's still flat and draining, sound edging that doesn't need to be pulled, and a straightforward rectangular yard. Where the old turf actually goes Turf is technically recyclable; plastics can be separated, melted and repelletized. In practice, most residential turf in Florida is hauled to a landfill or a construction-and-demolition debris facility, the same as old carpet, because separating fiber, backing and infill takes equipment most local waste operations don't run ( an industry overview of turf recycling ). We haven't found a synthetic-turf recycling program serving Central Florida as of September 2026. Landfilling isn't an oversight the state rule ignores, either: Rule 62-308.100 requires turf, backing and infill to be disposable at a Florida-permitted landfill under normal conditions, which is exactly where most of it ends up. Disposal is typically priced by weight; national guides put it around $60 to $70 a ton ( a synthetic grass disposal guide ), and a mid-size residential lawn's worth of old turf and infill adds up to a real number, part of a replacement quote rather than an afterthought. Bringing an older install up to the current rule A lot of turf around Kissimmee went in before Florida adopted Rule 62-308.100 on May 19, 2026, the first statewide minimum standard for synthetic turf on single-family lots ( Rule 62-308.100 ). Replacement is the natural moment to catch an older lawn up: a product with no intentionally added PFAS or heavy metals, a washed and open-graded base instead of whatever was under the original install, edges and seams anchored to handle wind and flooding, and irrigation heads capped rather than left running under the turf. If the old install sits inside a live oak's drip line, or closer than ten feet to a pond or canal without a seawall or bulkhead between them, replacement is also the moment to correct that footprint instead of repeating it. On a Poinciana or Harmony lot with a septic system, we also confirm the new layout leaves the tank's lid reachable for pump-out, easy to overlook on an install built before the rule existed. None of this requires a new permit from the state. Rule 62-308.100 sets a material and installation standard, and it says outright that it creates no new department-issued permit and doesn't touch easements or rights-of-way; what changed is what a compliant lawn has to look like, not who has to sign off on it. HOA paperwork the second time around An HOA that approved the original install years ago may still want to see the new one, especially if the community's design guidelines changed in the meantime or the visible footprint is different. What a Florida HOA can and can not restrict explains that a fenced backyard is generally protected from that review under F.S. 720.3045, while a front yard isn't. We prepare a fresh sample, spec sheet and site plan for the file when a community asks for one, same as on a first-time install. What a bad replacement job looks like The most common shortcut is skipping the base evaluation entirely and laying new turf over whatever's there, wet spots, soft spots and all, so the new lawn inherits the old lawn's problems on day one. Reusing edging that's already failed, cracked bender board, a paver border that's settled, saves a little money and costs more within a year when the new turf's edge lifts along it. Leaving old irrigation lines simply capped with tape instead of properly plugged is a leak waiting for the first hard rain to find it. After the new turf goes down Treat a replacement's first few months like a new install: keep heavy furniture off it while the base settles, rinse and brush on the same schedule as before, and walk the perimeter after the first real storm to check that every edge and seam is holding. Keep the product's spec sheet and the invoice describing the base work done; useful if an HOA ever asks again, and useful to us if a question comes up later about what's under the new lawn. Who is the best artificial turf replacement company near me? Ask to see the base before it's covered; a contractor confident in the work will show you the compacted material and the grade before the last roll of turf goes down. Ask what happens to the old turf and whether disposal is itemized in the quote. And ask directly whether the new install will meet the current state standard, anchored edges, capped irrigation, a PFAS-free product, since that's a fair baseline for anyone replacing turf in Florida now, not an upsell. We'll look at what's underneath before pricing anything, and tell you honestly if a repair would do instead. Osceola County Kissimmee Buenaventura Lakes Celebration St. Cloud Poinciana Reunion ChampionsGate Four Corners Harmony Orange County Hunters Creek Meadow Woods Southchase Lake Nona Dr. Phillips Polk County Davenport Questions people ask How do I know if my base needs to be rebuilt or just corrected? We probe it in several spots with a rod or a shovel. Firm, dry material that hasn't shifted usually just needs recompacting; soft, wet or spongy material in more than one spot means the base itself has failed and needs to come out and be rebuilt. Can the old turf be reused anywhere, like a dog run or a shed pad? Rarely for anything load-bearing or visible; UV-degraded fiber is brittle and the backing is usually near the end of its life too. It occasionally works as a temporary weed barrier under mulch, but that's a stretch, not a real second life. Does replacement turf need a permit if the original install didn't? Usually not a building permit, since it's the same use of the lot, but check with your city or county if the project also changes grading or drainage. An HOA that reviewed the first install may want to see the new one even without a government permit involved. How long does a typical replacement take? Two to five days for a residential yard, depending on how much of the base needs correcting. A yard where the base only needs light recompaction moves closer to a first-time install's timeline; one needing a full rebuild takes longer. Will a replacement match the rest of my landscaping if only part of the yard is worn out? We can often match pile height and color family to an adjoining area that's staying, though turf from a different production run is never a perfect color match. Full-yard replacement avoids the mismatch question entirely. Is it cheaper to replace turf myself and just hire out disposal? Removing the old turf yourself can trim some labor cost, but the base correction underneath is the part that determines how the new lawn performs, and that's harder to get right without the equipment and experience to grade and compact it properly. Does homeowners insurance ever cover turf replacement? Sometimes, for storm or fire damage specifically, rarely for ordinary wear from age and sun. Check your policy's language on landscaping or outdoor improvements before assuming either way, and keep the original install invoice in case a claim needs it.
